chapter.name: Work, Energy and Power
chapter.blurb: The chapter introduces the scalar product of two vectors and uses it to define the work done by a force, then relates work to kinetic energy through the work-energy theorem for constant and variable forces. It develops potential energy for conservative forces such as gravity and the spring force, and the conservation of mechanical energy. It ends with power and with elastic and inelastic collisions in one and two dimensions.

scope_in.item: Define the scalar product A.B = AB cos theta, interpret it as a projection, use its commutative and distributive properties and the unit-vector results, and evaluate it in components (AxBx + AyBy + AzBz) to find magnitudes, angles, projections and perpendicularity (Example 5.1)
State the work-energy theorem Kf - Ki = W for the net force, obtained from v^2 - u^2 = 2as, and use it to find the work done by an unknown force (Example 5.2)

Calculate the work done by a constant force as W = F d cos theta = F.d with its sign; state when no work is done; recognise positive and negative work; state the dimensions [M L^2 T^-2] and the unit joule; recognise that the works done by an action-reaction pair need not be equal and opposite (Example 5.3, Exercises 5.1, 5.2, 5.11)
Define kinetic energy K = (1/2) m v^2 as a scalar measuring the work a body can do by virtue of its motion, and relate changes in speed to changes in kinetic energy (Example 5.4, Exercise 5.12)
Find the work done by a variable force in one dimension as the sum of F(x) delta x, the area under the force-displacement curve (with sign) and the definite integral of F(x) dx (Example 5.5)

Follow the proof of the work-energy theorem for a variable force, apply it, and state that it is a scalar, integral form of Newton's second law carrying no explicit time or direction information (Example 5.6, Exercise 5.20)
Define gravitational potential energy V(h) = mgh for constant g, relate force and potential energy by F = -dV/dx, and state the three equivalent descriptions of a conservative force

State and apply the conservation of total mechanical energy K + V when only conservative forces do work: falling bodies, smooth inclines and tracks, pendulum bobs, and the bob in a vertical circle (Example 5.7, Exercises 5.6, 5.18)

State Hooke's law Fs = -kx, find the work done by the spring force and by the external force, use the spring potential energy V = (1/2) k x^2 and energy conservation for a block on a spring, including the maximum speed and maximum compression (Example 5.8, Exercise 5.4)

Recognise friction as a non-conservative force, use Ef - Ei = Wnc and the work-energy theorem when friction acts (Example 5.9), and state that the zero of potential energy is arbitrary but must be used consistently

Define average and instantaneous power, use P = W/t and P = F.v, the watt, the horse-power (1 hp = 746 W) and the kilowatt hour as a unit of energy; use the alternative energy units of Table 5.1 (Example 5.10, Exercises 5.9, 5.15, 5.23)

Explain why linear momentum is conserved in all collisions; distinguish elastic, inelastic and completely inelastic collisions; find the common velocity and the loss of kinetic energy in a completely inelastic collision in one dimension with one body at rest

Derive and use v1f = (m1 - m2) v1i/(m1 + m2) and v2f = 2 m1 v1i/(m1 + m2) for a head-on elastic collision with the second body at rest, with the equal-mass and heavy-target cases and the energy transfer to a moderator (Example 5.11)

Write the momentum and kinetic energy equations for a collision in two dimensions with one body at rest, count equations against unknowns, and use the result that equal masses in a glancing elastic collision move off at right angles (Example 5.12, Exercise 5.14)

concepts.name: The scalar product of two vectors
concepts.description: Definition A.B = AB cos theta, its meaning as a projection, its commutative and distributive properties, the unit-vector results and the component form AxBx + AyBy + AzBz.
concepts.idea: Two vectors can be multiplied to give a plain number: the magnitude of one times the component of the other along it.
concepts.rule: A.B = A B cos theta, where theta is the angle between A and B; the result is a scalar. B cos theta is the projection of B onto A and A cos theta is the projection of A onto B. A.B = B.A (commutative), A.(B + C) = A.B + A.C (distributive) and A.(lambda B) = lambda (A.B). For the unit vectors i.i = j.j = k.k = 1 and i.j = j.k = k.i = 0, so in components A.B = AxBx + AyBy + AzBz. A.A = A^2 = Ax^2 + Ay^2 + Az^2, and A.B = 0 if A and B are perpendicular.
concepts.example: For A = 2i + 3j + k and B = i - 2j + 4k, A.B = (2)(1) + (3)(-2) + (1)(4) = 0, so A and B are perpendicular.

concepts.name: Work done by a constant force
concepts.description: Work as W = F d cos theta = F.d, the conditions under which no work is done, positive and negative work, and the unit and dimensions of work.
concepts.idea: Work is done by a force on a body over a displacement; only the component of the force along the displacement counts, so work can be positive, negative or zero.
concepts.rule: W = (F cos theta) d = F.d, the product of the component of the force in the direction of the displacement and the magnitude of the displacement. No work is done if the displacement is zero, the force is zero, or the force and displacement are perpendicular. W is positive for theta between 0 and 90 degrees and negative for theta between 90 and 180 degrees; friction opposing the displacement (theta = 180 degrees) does negative work. Work is a scalar with dimensions [M L^2 T^-2] and SI unit joule (J). The work done on A by B is not necessarily equal and opposite to the work done on B by A.
concepts.example: A 50 N force acting at 60 degrees to a 4 m displacement does W = 50 x 4 x cos 60 degrees = 100 J; a 50 N force directly opposing the same displacement does -200 J.

concepts.name: Kinetic energy and the work-energy theorem
concepts.description: Kinetic energy K = (1/2) m v^2 as a positive scalar, and the work-energy theorem Kf - Ki = W for the work done by the net force, with what the theorem does and does not tell us.
concepts.idea: The work done on a body by the net force shows up as a change in the quantity (1/2) m v^2, which is called kinetic energy.
concepts.rule: K = (1/2) m v.v = (1/2) m v^2; it is a scalar, never negative, and measures the work a body can do by virtue of its motion. Work-energy (WE) theorem: the change in kinetic energy of a particle equals the work done on it by the net force, Kf - Ki = W. Positive net work increases K; negative net work decreases it. The theorem holds for a variable force too. It is an integral form of Newton's second law: it is a scalar relation and contains no explicit information about time or direction.
concepts.example: A body of mass 4 kg speeds up from 1 m/s to 3 m/s: Kf - Ki = (1/2)(4)(9) - (1/2)(4)(1) = 16 J, so the net force did 16 J of work on it.

questions.a: (a) Net force during the pull = 13 - 4 = 9 N along the motion, so net work = 9 x 4 = 36 J = (1/2)(2) v^2 - 0, giving v^2 = 36 and v = 6 m/s. (b) After the pull is removed only friction does work: -4 x d = 0 - 36 J, so d = 9 m.

concepts.name: Potential energy, conservative forces and the conservation of mechanical energy
concepts.description: Gravitational potential energy V = mgh, the relation F = -dV/dx, the three descriptions of a conservative force, and K + V = constant applied to falling bodies, smooth inclines and a bob moving in a vertical circle.
concepts.idea: Work done against a conservative force such as gravity is stored as potential energy and can be recovered as kinetic energy, so the sum of the two stays constant.
concepts.rule: Gravitational potential energy at height h (g constant, zero at the chosen reference level) is V(h) = mgh, the negative of the work done by the gravitational force in raising the body. For a conservative force in one dimension F(x) = -dV/dx, and the change in potential energy equals the negative of the work done by the force. A force is conservative if its work depends only on the end points, equivalently if its work round a closed path is zero. If only conservative forces do work, Ki + V(xi) = Kf + V(xf): the total mechanical energy K + V is conserved. For a ball dropped from height H, v^2 = 2g(H - h) at height h. The zero of potential energy is arbitrary but must be kept fixed.
concepts.example: A stone of mass 2 kg is dropped from a height of 20 m (ground as zero, g = 10 m/s^2): V = 2 x 10 x 20 = 400 J at the top, so K = 400 J at the ground and v = sqrt(2 x 10 x 20) = 20 m/s.

concepts.name: Potential energy of a spring and non-conservative forces
concepts.description: Hooke's law Fs = -kx, the work done by the spring force, the elastic potential energy (1/2) k x^2, energy exchange for a block on a spring, and the change in mechanical energy when friction acts.
concepts.idea: A stretched or compressed spring stores energy that depends only on how far it is from its natural length; friction, by contrast, takes mechanical energy away for good.
concepts.rule: For an ideal light spring Fs = -kx, where x is the displacement from the equilibrium (natural-length) position and k (in N/m) is the spring constant. The work done by the spring force in an extension or compression of size xm from the natural length is -(1/2) k xm^2, and from xi to xf it is (1/2) k xi^2 - (1/2) k xf^2; in a cyclic process it is zero, so the spring force is conservative. With V = 0 at the natural length, V(x) = (1/2) k x^2. For a block released from rest at extension xm on a smooth surface, (1/2) k xm^2 = (1/2) k x^2 + (1/2) m v^2, and the maximum speed, at x = 0, is vm = sqrt(k/m) xm. Friction is non-conservative: Ef - Ei = Wnc, where Wnc is the work done by the non-conservative force and depends on the path.
concepts.example: A spring of spring constant 300 N/m stretched by 0.1 m from its natural length stores V = (1/2)(300)(0.1)^2 = 1.5 J.

concepts.name: Collisions: momentum conservation and the completely inelastic collision in one dimension
concepts.description: Why total linear momentum is conserved in every collision, the difference between elastic, inelastic and completely inelastic collisions, and the common velocity and loss of kinetic energy when two bodies stick together in one dimension.
concepts.idea: In any collision the total momentum of the two bodies is unchanged, but kinetic energy survives in full only if the collision is elastic; when the bodies stick together, the most is lost.
concepts.rule: During a collision the mutual forces are equal and opposite at every instant (Newton's third law), so the changes in momentum cancel and the total linear momentum is conserved in all collisions. Total kinetic energy is not necessarily conserved. Elastic collision: the initial and final kinetic energies are equal. Completely inelastic collision: the two bodies move together afterwards. Inelastic collision: the deformation is partly relieved and some kinetic energy is lost. For m1 moving at v1i striking m2 at rest and sticking, in one dimension, m1 v1i = (m1 + m2) vf, so vf = m1 v1i/(m1 + m2), and the loss in kinetic energy is (1/2) [m1 m2/(m1 + m2)] v1i^2.
concepts.example: A trolley of mass 4 kg moving at 3 m/s sticks to a stationary trolley of mass 2 kg: vf = 4 x 3/(4 + 2) = 2 m/s, and the kinetic energy falls from 18 J to 12 J.

concepts.name: Elastic collisions in one and two dimensions
concepts.description: The final velocities in a head-on elastic collision with a body at rest, the equal-mass and heavy-target special cases, the transfer of kinetic energy to a moderator nucleus, and the momentum and energy equations for a two-dimensional collision.
concepts.idea: In an elastic collision both the total momentum and the total kinetic energy are the same before and after, and these two conditions fix the final velocities in a head-on collision.
concepts.rule: Head-on (one-dimensional) elastic collision of m1 moving at v1i with m2 at rest: m1 v1i = m1 v1f + m2 v2f and m1 v1i^2 = m1 v1f^2 + m2 v2f^2 give v2f = v1i + v1f, v1f = (m1 - m2) v1i/(m1 + m2) and v2f = 2 m1 v1i/(m1 + m2). Equal masses: v1f = 0 and v2f = v1i. If m2 is much greater than m1: v1f is nearly -v1i and v2f nearly 0. Fraction of kinetic energy transferred to m2: 4 m1 m2/(m1 + m2)^2. In two dimensions: m1 v1i = m1 v1f cos theta1 + m2 v2f cos theta2 and 0 = m1 v1f sin theta1 - m2 v2f sin theta2, with (1/2) m1 v1i^2 = (1/2) m1 v1f^2 + (1/2) m2 v2f^2 if elastic; one of the four unknowns must be known. Equal masses in a glancing elastic collision with one at rest move off at right angles.
concepts.example: A ball of mass 4 kg moving at 5 m/s collides elastically head-on with a ball of mass 1 kg at rest: v1f = (4 - 1) x 5/(4 + 1) = 3 m/s and v2f = 2 x 4 x 5/(4 + 1) = 8 m/s.
